title: Boosting the energy density of graphene supercapacitors by using sustainable/natural black-iron-sand
abstract: Abstract Supercapacitor (SCs) were fabricated using black iron-sand (BS) as redox-powder (composed mainly of SiO 2 /magnetite). In addition, it was studied the effect of two electrolytes (seawater (SW) and PVA/H 3 PO 4  (AD) mixture) on the SC performance. Electrochemical characterizations revealed that the BS(AD)-SC device (made with acidic electrolyte and BS) reached a capacitance of 668.66 F/g and energy density of 92.7 Wh/kg, while the BS(SW)-SC device (made with seawater (SW) electrolyte and BS), produced capacitance and energy density of 282.24 F/g and 39.2 Wh/kg, respectively. Reference SCs were fabricated without iron-sand powder, but contained SW or AD electrolytes. Those devices produced much lower capacitances of 54–94.1 F/g. Thus, adding BS to SCs increased the capacitance by 6-11.3 times. According to XPS/Raman analyses, BS powder contained oxygen vacancy defects, Si 4+  and Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ species, which worked as redox-centers for charge storage. Consequently, devices made with BS had CV with intense redox peaks, while devices made without BS had a quasi-rectangular shape (stored charge only by electronic-double layer). Moreover, diffusion coefficient was calculated for devices made with acidic and seawater electrolyte and obtained values of 9.51 × 10⁻⁸ cm²/s, and 4.57 × 10⁻⁸ cm²/s, respectively. Thus, the ion-transport/charge-storage in SCs electrodes was more efficient by using the acidic electrolyte. Also, electrochemical performance of the BS(AD)-SC device was evaluated at 70 °C. At this temperature, the capacitance was slightly higher (684.2 F/g) and this occurred because heating increased the mobility of ions through the BS-based electrodes. This research demonstrated that using black sand (natural/abundant resource) is promising to build low-cost supercapacitors.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Currently, a large number of electronic products, such as mobile phones, tablets, and smartwatches, require high-capacity batteries for long operation times. Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are the most popular devices for storing energy in the electrical industry. However, lithium-ion batteries have certain problems: they are large, heavy, and rigid, and they are not thermally stable. They can only be charged and discharged 100–300 times and are made with toxic lithium salts [ 1 ]. These limitations have driven the development of other advanced energy storage technologies. In particular, the supercapacitor (SC), an electrical device that stores charge through faradic and double-layer processes, has recently captured the attention of modern industry [ 2 ]. This device has become an option for energy storage, given the interest in clean technologies and sustainable energy sources. These devices are lighter and more flexible than lithium-ion batteries. Furthermore, supercapacitors (SCs) offer significant advantages over lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), such as greater energy storage capacity in a smaller size, as well as faster charge and discharge rates. These components are ideal for portable electronics, as they combine efficiency and compact size, essential characteristics for portable applications. In addition, SCs support up to 20,000 charge-discharge cycles and have simpler designs. Nevertheless, SCs are not suitable for devices requiring prolonged operation, as they do not store as much energy as lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) [ 3 ]. Consequently, research is currently being carried out to overcome these limitations. For this last purpose, Ni-based materials have been reported to enhance the performance of supercapacitors. For example, Randive et al. [ 4 ,  5 ] prepared nickel oxide (NiO) electrodes optimized at 0.8 M (NiO@AC-4), which demonstrated a maximum specific capacitance of 256.32 F/g at a scan rate of 0.002 V/s. The electrodes exhibited an energy density of 29.08 Wh/kg, a power density of 3.06 kW/kg, and capacitance retention of 69.42% after 5,000 cycles of charge-discharge. Also, the same research group synthesized a porous NiCo₂O₄ electrode via spray pyrolysis which produced a specific capacitance of 676.82 F/g and had capacitance retention of 89.23% after 5000 cycles of charge-discharge [ 5 ]. The asymmetric device made with NiCo₂O₄@graphite reached a maximum energy density of 3249.6 Wh/kg and a capacitance of 675.72 F/g. Moreover, graphite has been used for the design and simulation of asymmetric NiO@Graphite based supercapacitors, which utilized a nickel oxide electrode optimized by pyrolysis at 375 °C. The optimum device demonstrated a maximum specific capacitance of 256.52 F/g by cyclic voltammetry and 18.60 F/g by galvanostatic charge-discharge curves [ 6 ]. Similarly, another compound such as NiO@KOH have employed to fabricate supercapacitors which produced maximum capacitance of 1180.95 F/g (at 0.005 V/s) [ 7 ]. This last work also reported a symmetric device made with NiO@NiO and this one had a capacitance of 411.58 F/g. Furthermore, it has been published one work that explored the use of different alcohols (methanol, ethanol, and propanol) as solvents in the synthesis of nickel oxide films for asymmetric supercapacitors. The optimized device utilized Nickel oxide films synthesized with methanol and produced a maximum capacitance of 113.67 F/g [ 8 ].

On the other hand, pollution has increased considerably due to the greater production of solid waste, such as metals and plastics. The accumulation of this trash significantly affects the environment, contaminating plants and causing the death of animals in various locations [ 9 ]. Supercapacitors (SCs) made with recycled polymers represent an attempt to offer a reusable and low-cost alternative [ 10 ]. These recycled polymers (plastics) serve as a substrate to print electrodes, which are utilized in the construction of SCs. To operate correctly, the electrodes must be made of highly conductive materials that allow the movement and extraction of electrons. Carbon materials, such as graphene and the other derivatives, are frequently used as supercapacitor electrodes due to their excellent electrical conductivity [ 11 ]. Graphene has generated significant interest because of its remarkable mechanical/optical properties. The internal structure is a two-dimensional carbon monolayer with an array of sp²-hybridized carbon atoms, exhibiting some of the most intriguing properties. This material has a high electrical conductivity, a large specific surface area of 2630 m²/g, and a low density of 2.28 g/cm³ [ 12 ,  13 – 14 ]. Regarding the use of graphene for the construction of SCs, the following works stand out in the literature for their contribution, such as: Vivekchand et al. [ 15 ] synthesized graphene by exfoliation of graphitic oxide, which reached a specific capacitance of 117 F/g and an energy density of 31.9 Wh/kg. Dai et al. [ 16 ] introduced an efficient and scalable method for the production of N-doped graphene electrodes, achieving a specific capacitance value of approximately 390 F/g. These electrodes showed an energy density of 55 Wh/kg, and they were tested for 20,000 charge and discharge cycles and exhibited 96.6% of their initial capacity. Le Fevre et al. [ 17 ] produced graphene oxide (GO) electrodes, which exhibited a specific capacitance of 154 F/g, with a cyclability greater than 95% after 10,000 charge/discharge cycles. Down et al. [ 18 ] reported a facile fabrication of a graphene-oxide (GO)-based supercapacitor. The SC device showed a high specific capacitive performance value of 423 F/g. The device also exhibits an energy density of 11.6 Wh/kg and a power density of 13.9 kW/kg. Tian et al. [ 19 ] presented the preparation of hydrophilic graphene/graphene oxide nanosheets (hG/GO-Nsheet) as SC electrodes. The composite device exhibited a specific capacitance of 483 F /g at 1 A/g; also, the composite SC demonstrated a high energy density of 17.9 Wh /kg at a power density of 500 W /kg. On the other hand, recent studies suggest that the use of graphene combined with porous materials has the potential to significantly improve the performance of SCs. In particular, the use of silica (SiO₂) in the fabrication of SCs is due to the substantial surface area, which improves the ion storage capacity of the electrolyte [ 20 ]. Several works have documented the fabrication of SCs utilizing graphene and SiO₂: For example, Lo et al. [ 21 ] presented a method to make a C/SiO₂-based SC with outstanding cycle capacitance retention above 95%. Furthermore, they used carbon materials to create the SC electrodes. A specific capacitance value of 298 F/g was achieved, along with a high retention rate of 91.53% after 1000 cycles of charge-discharge. The energy density is measured at 26.25 Wh/kg when the current density is set at 1 A/g. Ristriana et al. [ 22 ] synthesized a composite of reduced graphene oxide and nanosilica (rGO/N-SiO₂) using the hydrothermal method to fabricate supercapacitor electrodes. The RGO/N-SiO₂ exhibited a specific capacitance of 166.9 F/g and an energy density of 23.2 Wh/kg. In addition, the electrode demonstrated excellent stability, at 95.51%, after 4000 charge-discharge cycles. Moreover, magnetite (Fe 3 O 4 ) is another promising material for SC applications. The charge storage occurs through rapid and reversible redox reactions involving Fe³⁺⇌Fe²⁺ ions in the bulk of the magnetite, which plays a crucial role in enhancing energy storage capacity in the SC [ 23 ,  24 ]. Among the notable works, we found: Patil et al. [ 25 ] prepared a combination of reduced graphene oxide (rGO) with magnetite (Fe₃O₄)-NH-polyaniline (PANI) nanocomposite. The rGO-Fe₃O₄-NH-PANI nanocomposite exhibited a specific capacitance of 336.4 F/g and an energy density of 11.81 Wh/Kg with a power density of 1258.3 W/Kg. It also maintained a capacitance retention of approximately 98% after 2000 charge/discharge cycles. Sanei et al. [ 26 ] used a Fe₃O₄ nanocomposite with a uniformly ferromagnetic nickel foam (NF) as an electrode material. This nanocomposite demonstrated a high specific capacitance of 656.7 F/g at 1 A/g, with an exceptional energy density of 103.3 Wh/kg at a power density of 750 W/kg and excellent cyclic stability (83.61% capacity retention) after 10,000 charge/discharge cycles. Manikandan et al. [ 27 ] synthesized porous flower-like magnetite (Fe₃O₄) nanostructures as electrode material. The as-prepared porous nanostructure presented a specific capacitance value of 183 F/g at 1 A/g with a capacitance retention of 65% after 5000 charge/discharge cycles. Jian et al. [ 28 ] synthesized a magnetite nanocomposite with reduced graphene oxide (Fe₃O 4 /rGO). The nanocomposite achieved a specific capacitance of 317.4 F/g at a current density of 0.5 A/g. Furthermore, it showed high cyclic stability, maintaining a capacity retention of 86.9% after 5500 charge/discharge cycles. As observed from the previous results for devices made with SiO 2 -based or Fe-based composite electrodes, the values of energy density are low in general (< 110 Wh/kg) and such composites are formed by expensive polymers or their fabrication involves complex synthesis. In addition, most devices made with such composite electrodes are not flexible, which limits their use for flexible electronics. Hence, it is necessary to develop low-cost composite electrodes for the massive fabrication of flexible SCs.

A promising candidate of redox material for SC electrodes is the volcanic iron sand (also named black sand, labeled in this work as BS), which is rich in magnetite and silica. This type of sand is abundant on the Pacific coast of Mexico, and it represents a low-cost material that can be used to improve SCs. The dark color in BS comes from the high concentration of magnetic minerals from volcanic or eroded sources [ 29 ]. To enhance the energy storage in the SCs, the BS was utilized as a redox powder in this research. This black sand was acquired from Playa El Real, located in Tecomán, Colima, México. On the other hand, the use of an acidic electrolyte in the supercapacitors over extended periods generates H₂ gas, as indicated in the literature, which can lead to inflation and potential damage to the device [ 30 ]. To address this issue and create environmentally friendly (non-toxic) devices, we used seawater (SW) as an electrolyte source. The seawater presents numerous benefits compared to acidic electrolytes: it is abundantly accessible (lowering the cost of supercapacitors), eco-friendly, and comprises ions like sodium, potassium, calcium, and magnesium, which are suitable for redox reactions involved in charge storage [ 31 ]. The supercapacitor constructed with graphene-based electrodes, utilizing black sand (BS) as a redox powder and seawater (SW) as the electrolyte, demonstrated a specific capacitance of 282.24 F/g and an energy density of 39.2 Wh/kg. Moreover, the device that used the acidic electrolyte (AD) showed an outstanding performance of 668.66 F/g and 92.7 Wh/kg. Additionally, the SCs operated at high temperatures during the electrochemical tests and bending cycles to evaluate their robustness. At a high operating temperature of 70 °C, it showed an increase in the electrochemical properties with specific capacitance and energy density values of 684.2 F/g and 95.1 Wh/kg, respectively. Also, the device presented a capacitance retention of 92% after 1000 charge/discharge cycles, demonstrating great durability and efficiency.

Overall the main novelties of this work are the following: (i) the use for the first time of black sand (BS) as a redox powder for SC applications; (ii) the use of the combination of the black sand (redox powder) and seawater (electrolyte) at the same time to construct ecofriendly and low-cost SCs; (iii) we report electrochemical tests at elevated temperatures, which has been poorly studied in the literature; and (iv) the capacitive/diffusive behavior of the energy storage in the SCs along with ion kinetics between the SC electrodes was studied for the two electrolytes (acid and seawater) used in the devices. In general, the use of two renewable/abundant resources, black sand (BS) and saltwater (SW), sets a standard for using efficient capacitive materials for the development of energy storage devices that are ecologically benign upon disposal. Also, this work found that using black sand, a natural and abundant resource, is an advantageous way to build low-cost energy storage devices, which have high electrochemical performance for portable/wearable electronics.

sections.heading: Preparation of redox powder based on black sand
paragraphs: The black sand (BS) was collected from Playa El Real (18.8717° N and 103.9161° W) located in Tecomán, Colima, México. BS was selected, cleaned, and filtered to remove organic impurities and put in a drying oven to eliminate the rest of the moisture. The material was grained in a mortar to obtain a fine black powder and again thermally treated for 2 h. After that, the powder was permitted to cool before its use as a redox powder on the graphene-based electrodes.

sections.heading: Assembling for SCs
paragraphs: The construction of the graphene-based electrodes was carried out as follows: first, rectangular pieces of recycled polyethylene (PE), measuring 2.0 cm by 3.0 cm, were used. Next, graphene ink was applied to the recycled substrate using a blade-coating method [ 32 ], and the resulting graphene-based electrode was labeled as G-E. After that, copper strips were connected to the graphene-based electrodes, and the cellulose paper separator was impregnated with a PVA/H₃PO₄-based electrolyte. The electrolyte was prepared by mixing distilled water, PVA, and H₃PO₄ in a weight ratio of 1:0.2:0.8. Seawater was also used as an environmentally friendly source of electrolytes. The electrode underwent a coating process using the blade coating technique with the BS redox powder. This resulting electrode was designated as BS-E. Later, the dielectric separator impregnated with the acidic electrolyte (250 µl) was placed between two electrodes (sandwiched) and encapsulated with an epoxy resin. The supercapacitor (SC) fabricated with pure graphene-based electrodes and a PVA/H₃PO₄ electrolyte (referred to as AD in this work) is designated G(AD)-SC. The device fabricated with seawater electrolyte (250 µl) and graphene-based electrodes is designated G(SW)-SC. The seawater electrolyte was obtained from a Mexican beach named Puerto Vallarta (see the chemical composition for seawater in Table S1 of the supporting information). The electrical conductivity for the seawater was measured using a conductivity meter (HANNA Instruments) and obtained a value of 58,840 µS/cm. The pH for the seawater was 7.7. The SC fabricated with graphene electrodes, BS redox powder, and an acidic electrolyte (AD) is designated BS(AD)-SC. The device using the same components (graphene electrodes and BS redox powder) but with seawater as the electrolyte is designated BS(SW)-SC.

sections.heading: Characterization of supercapacitor electrodes using: SEM, XRD, UV-Vis, FTIR, Raman, and XPS techniques
paragraphs: We employed a scanning electron microscope (SEM-QUANTA 250 model), which was operated at 15 kV to study the surface morphology of the electrodes. The SEM is equipped with an integrated energy dispersive detector (EDS) that facilitates elemental analysis. Additionally, X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) was used to examine the crystalline phase of the materials on the electrodes, using a Rigaku X-ray diffractometer (Cu-alpha wavelength of 1.54056 Å). The XRD spectra were obtained throughout the 2θ range of 15–70°. Also, a Carry 5000 spectrometer was used to collect the absorbance bands for UV-Vis examination within the range of 210–750 nm. However, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) was necessary to detect the chemical components on the electrode surfaces. The survey was performed in the spectral region of 450–4000 cm⁻¹, using a Shimadzu IR-tracer spectrophotometer. The Renishaw micro-Raman apparatus was used to acquire Raman spectra; measurements were performed at a wavelength of 532 nm, covering the range of 1000–2000 cm⁻¹. Finally, the chemical species on the electrodes were then identified using Thermo Scientific K-alpha equipment for X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS).

For this research, the active mass for the graphene layer was 5.7 ± 0.1 mg, the active mass for the redox powder (black-sand) was 65 ± 2 mg. Thus, the total active mass for charge storage per SC electrode was 70.7 mg (this mass does not include the mass for plastic substrate, copper collectors or encapsulation). The thickness of the redox layer deposited on the graphene electrode was 70 ± 2 μm.

sections.heading: Morphological and structural characterization for SC electrodes
paragraphs: Figure  1 a presents the SEM image for a graphene-based electrode. The graphene layer (G) applied to the polyethylene substrate consists of stacked graphene microplates, which have average dimensions of 2 × 3.5 μm² (refer to the red square). The aggregated graphene microplates established a conductive pathway for charge transport. Nonetheless, certain irregularities, such as cracks (blue arrow) or holes (yellow arrow), were noted on the graphene layer in the G-E electrode.
Fig. 1 SEM images for: ( a ) G-E electrode, ( b ) BS powder, ( c ) BS based electrode (BS-E) and ( d ) EDS spectrum for the BS powder

In Fig.  1 b, we can observe the mineral grains with an average size of 3.5 μm² (red circles). Also in the image, bigger grains are observed too (see yellow arrow). In contrast. Figure  1 c presents the image of the BS-E electrode. The image showed an empty surface in a dark color that corresponds to the graphene base (red arrow) in the electrode, while over its surface we can see the black sand grains with different shapes (blue arrow). Furthermore, Fig.  1 d displays the EDS spectrum of the black sand (BS). The detection of carbon (C), aluminum (Al), calcium (Ca), and manganese (Mg), along with other elements identified in the study, such as phosphorus (P) and sodium (Na), as well as the presence of iron (Fe) and a pronounced peak of silicon (Si), confirms the elemental composition of this sand, which has a volcanic origin [ 29 ].

On the other hand, X-ray diffraction analysis was essential for identifying the various phases of the material used as redox powder in the graphene-based electrodes, particularly the black sand (BS). The XRD pattern for the G-E electrode is illustrated in Fig.  2 a. The diffraction peaks observed at 21.5°, 23.7°, 38.8°, 44.6°, and 65.1° that are associated with the orientations of polyethylene (PE) [ 35 ]. The peak located at 26.6° corresponds to the (002) plane, which is attributed to the graphene phase [ 36 ]. The results above show that we have an electrode with a polyethylene base and graphene. Figure  2 b displays the XRD pattern for the BS-E electrode. Clear diffraction peaks appear at 2θ values of 21.7°, 26.6°, 54.8°, and 66.9°. These peaks closely match the reference pattern for SiO₂, as indicated by JCPDS card No. 99 − 0088. Additional peaks were noted at 2θ values of 20.1°, 23.7°, 27.9°, 30.7°, 35.7°, 42.6°, 46.3°, 52.4°, 56.6°, and 62.3°, which correspond to magnetite according to JCPDS card No. 01-075-0449. Moreover, spurious phases are observed and correspond to metallic aluminum (JCPDS No. 04-0787), with peaks at 38.5°, 44.8°, and 65.2°. This last phase appeared because it was a component of the recycled plastic (substrate) utilized to fabricate the SC electrodes. Also, the calcite (CaCO₃) phase (JCPDS No. 82-1690), with peaks at 28.3°, 31°, 38.1°, and 54.5°; and, less prominently, the graphene phase, which appears at 26.5° were also observed. Thus, we can confirm that we have an electrode composed of BS and graphene. These findings indicate a complex mineral composition that may influence the electrochemical performance of the supercapacitor and promote energy storage. These findings indicate a complex mineral composition in the black sand that may influence the electrochemical performance of the supercapacitor to promote the energy storage.

Fig. 2 a ,  b  are the XRD patterns for the G-E and BS-based electrodes, respectively.  c  displays the FTIR spectra for the BS-E electrodes before and after their utilization in devices made with acidic and seawater electrolytes

sections.heading: FTIR analysis for SC electrodes
paragraphs: The functional groups of the black sand (BS) electrodes were analyzed using Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectra within the range of 500–4000 cm⁻¹. FTIR spectroscopy was employed to identify oxygen functional groups, such as hydroxyl and carbonyl. These groups significantly improve charge transfer and increase the capacitance of the electrodes [ 37 ]. Figure  2 c presents the FTIR spectra for the BS-E, BS(SW)-E, and BS(AD)-E electrodes. The black curve corresponds to the BS-E electrode. The spectrum shows a series of peaks at specific locations: 3675, 2973, 1726, 1394, 1054, and 543 cm⁻¹, which are attributed to O-H stretching vibrations of hydroxyl functional groups in the mineral structure (which indicates absorbed water molecules); C-H stretching vibrations; stretching vibrations of the carbonyl group (C=O); carbonate ion stretching vibration (CO₃²⁻); Si-O asymmetric stretching vibrations; and the last signal is attributed to the magnetite (Fe₃O₄) in the black sand, respectively [ 38 ,  39 ,  40 ,  41 ,  42 – 43 ]. Subsequently, the blue spectrum corresponds to the BS(SW)-E electrode; this electrode has the black sand (BS) and the seawater as electrolyte (SW). A peak was observed at 3590 cm⁻¹, which is ascribed to the hydroxyl group (-OH); small signals were observed at 2986 and 2381 cm⁻¹, attributed to the stretching vibrations of C-H due to the organic compounds attached to the black sand. However, the peaks identified at 1639, 1442, and 1075 correspond to O-H bending vibrations of water molecules, the presence of carbonate minerals, and Si-O asymmetric stretching vibrations, in the given order [ 44 ,  45 – 46 ]. The last two peaks, 698 and 626 cm⁻¹, are associated with the Fe-O/Fe-OH vibration of the magnetite phase, and the last can be attributed to Al-O coordination or coupling between O-Si-O bending and K-O stretching vibrations, which may be characteristic of feldspar, which is also a common component of the sand [ 47 ]. The red spectrum in Fig.  2 c is ascribed to the BS(AD)-E electrode, which was made with the black sand and the acidic electrolyte. An absorption band from 3681 to 2546 cm⁻¹ is noted, which is associated with the existence of hydroxyl groups (-OH) from water (either adsorbed or inside minerals such as clays/hydroxides), while the small signal observed at 2386 cm⁻¹ is due to the stretching vibrations of C-H. The peak at 1633 is related to the O-H bending vibrations of water molecules, and the broad peak located at 964 cm⁻¹ is often ascribed to the existence of silicate minerals and frequently associated with Si-O stretching vibrations [ 48 ].

sections.heading: The electrochemical performance of the supercapacitors
paragraphs: Figure  3 a presents the cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves at four different sweep rates and a voltage window of 1.0 V for the G(SW)-SC supercapacitor, which utilizes graphene-based electrodes in conjunction with seawater (SW) as the electrolyte (in the inset, a digital image of the SC in Fig.  3 a).
Fig. 3 CV curves for: ( a ) G(SW)-SC, ( b ) G(AD)-SC, ( c ) BS(SW)-SC and ( d ) BS(AD)-SC devices

The CV curves are thin, and no redox shoulders were observed, indicating that the energy storage in the device is attributed to the EDL process [ 49 ]. Next, Fig.  3 b displays the CV curve for the G(AD)-SC device, constructed with graphene-based electrodes and the acidic electrolyte made with H₃PO₄. As we observed the CV curves, they displayed an increase in width of approximately 50% compared with the CV curves in Fig.  3 a. In addition, Fig.  3 c illustrates CV curves of the BS(SW)-SC supercapacitor. This device uses the black sand (BS) powder as a redox powder and the seawater as the electrolyte. A significant increase in the width of the CV curves is observed during the electrochemical process, compared with Fig.  3 a and b. These results indicate that the BS(SW)-SC device exhibits superior electrochemical performance with the inclusion of the BS as a redox powder. A small redox shoulder was observed at approximately 0.6, indicating that the energy storage in the BC-SCAP device is due to a redox reactions involving the BS powder [ 50 ]. The BS(SW)-SC shows a curve width increase of about 500% compared to the CV curve presented by the G(SW)-SC device. This increase in size could indicate that the interaction between the black sand and the seawater components improves the electrochemical performance. However, the use of the acidic electrolyte (AC) and the back sand (BS) improved the performance of the BS(AD)-SC device. The device presented in Fig.  3 d showed a double size of the CV curve width compared with the device BS(SW)-SC. A redox shoulder was observed approximately at 0.7 V, which indicates that the energy storage in the BS(AD)-SC is mainly caused by redox reactions. In contrast, Fig.  4 a depicts the GCD curves at a current density of 1 A/g for the four supercapacitors: G(SW)-SC, G(AD)-SC, BS(SW)-SC, and BS(AD)-SC. The GCD curves showed output voltages of 0.030 V, 0.035 V, 0.050 V, and 0.135 V after 10 h of discharge, respectively. As observed the devices made with black-sand had the slowest discharge times and the BS(AD)-SC device produced the highest output voltage of 0.135 V after 10 h of discharge. For completeness, Fig. S1 in supporting information showed the complete curve of discharge for the two best devices made with black-iron sand. From there, we realized that the BS(SW)-SC, and BS(AD)-SC devices are completely discharged after 18.4 and 20.7 h, respectively. The specific capacitance (Cs) and energy density (Ed) values were calculated using Eqs. (1) and (2) in Sect.  2.4  along with the GCD plots in Fig.  4 a.

Fig. 4 a  GCD curves for the G(SW)-SC, G(AD)-SC, BS(SW)-SC and BS(AD)-SC devices.  b  shows the capacitance retention vs. cycles of charge discharge for the BS(SW)-SC and BS(SW)-SC devices.  c  shows the capacitive and diffusion contributions for the charge storage in the BS(SW)-SC device.  d  shows the I p  vs. V 1/2  plot for the calculation of diffusion coefficient

As a result, G(SW)-SC, G(AD)-SC, BS(SW)-SC, and BS(AD)-SC presented specific-capacitance-energy density (C s -E d ) values of 54.44 F/g-12.7 Wh/kg, 94.1 F/g-21.8 Wh/kg, 282.24 F/g-39.2 Wh/kg, and 668.66 F/g-92.7 Wh/kg, respectively. For completeness, the specific capacities were calculated in terms of Coulombs per gram (C/g). The equation utilized for the calculation of capacity is presented in Section S1 of supporting information. Consequently, the best two devices BS(SW)-SC, and BS(AD)-SC had capacities of 211.68 C/g and 581.73 C/g, respectively. The values of electrochemical parameters above revealed a remarkable improvement for the energy storage capacity, especially for the BS(AD) composite, which shows an impressive synergy to further elevate the specific capacitance and energy density values. Furthermore, we can observe the structural integrity that the BS-E electrodes retain after being soaked with acidic and seawater electrolytes; that is, the phase of the electrode materials did not change (see XRD pattern for the BS(AD)-E and BS(SW)-E electrodes in Fig. S2a of supporting information).

To evaluate the stability of the tested supercapacitors, 1000 charge and discharge cycles were performed (see Fig.  4 b). As a result, the capacitance retention values for BS(SW)-SC and BS(AD)-SC decreased from 100% to 91.8% and from 100% to 95%, respectively. The results indicate that, although BS(AD)-SC exhibits a minimum decrease in capacitance retention after the cycles, it demonstrates superior performance compared to the supercapacitor using seawater as the electrolyte. The capacitance retention of the BS(SW)-SC and BS(AD)-SC devices was also analyzed under mechanical stress; 1000 bending cycles were performed. Fig. S2b (see the supplementary Information) shows a decrease in capacitance from 100% to 90% and from 100% to 92%, respectively (a digital image of the SC in a bent position is presented in the inset of Fig. S2b). Overall, both devices demonstrated robust construction, with only a maximum of 10% loss in capacitance retention. In Table  1 , a summary of electrochemical parameters for SC cited in this work can be observed and compared with the results obtained in this investigation. The capacitive and diffusive behavior of the best device, BS(AD)-SC, was investigated. The cyclic voltammetry curves were analyzed using Dunn’s method [ 51 ], as detailed in Section S2 of the supporting information (Eqs. (2) and (3)), at a fixed potential of 0.65 V. This analysis yielded a b-value of 0.72 (see Fig. S2c in the supporting information), which falls between the optimal capacitive value of 1.0 and the diffusion-controlled value of 0.5. This data suggests a hybrid storage mechanism, indicating that both capacitive and diffusive processes significantly contribute to charge storage. The material accumulates charge through capacitive reactions at the surface level and via ion diffusion at the bulk level. Such hybrid behavior is commonly observed in these materials, which store charge through redox reactions at the surface while also incorporating slower ionic diffusion throughout the bulk [ 52 ]. Subsequently, the capacitive and diffusive contributions of the total stored energy were calculated using equations from the supporting information (4) and (5). Figure  4 c presents a bar chart illustrating the hybrid contributions at sweep rates of 25, 50, 75, and 100 mV/s. The diffusive contributions were found to be 70.0%, 62.3%, 57.4%, and 53.9%, respectively. However, the graph demonstrates that diffusive contributions decrease as the sweep rate increases, suggesting that higher rates may favor capacitive behavior over diffusive transport mechanisms.

On the other hand, to determine the ion transport rate between the active materials (redox powder and electrolyte) within the electrode, the diffusion coefficient D was calculated using cyclic voltammetry and the Randles-Sevcik equation [ 53 ] (see Section S3 and Eq. (6) of the supporting information). Figure  4 d shows a linear fit of the square root of the voltage sweep rate ( v 1/2 ) against the anodic peak current (ip) obtained from the CV curves. For the active redox material presented in the black sand (the magnetite), employ the Randles-Sevcik equation and the resulting slope value of 0.59721 in the linear fit. The calculation considered a working area of 12 cm² (2 × 2 cm x 3 cm), which is the total area covered by two electrodes; room temperature (25 °C); and a molar C concentration of the electrolyte of 1 M for the acidic electrolyte (H₃PO₄) and, considering 0.6 M for the seawater, a total mass charge of 35 mg deposited on the electrode, and assuming 60% of magnetite in the total mass of the black sand (a typical percentage of magnetite in this type of volcanic sand), the other 40% is impurities and silica. The theoretical value obtained was D = 9.51 × 10⁻⁸ cm²/s, which represents the effective diffusion of protons from phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) within the magnetite solid matrix in the black sand (see a schematic representation in Fig.  5 a to visualize the ion diffusion through the BS based electrodes). Instead, the resulting value for the use of seawater as an electrolyte is D = 4.57 × 10⁻⁸ cm²/s, which is approximately half of the value obtained for the use of the acidic electrolyte. In acidic (H₃PO₄) media, protons (H⁺) are the primary charge carriers.

Fig. 5 a  Diagram showing the storage of charge in BS-based SCs.  b ,  c  are Nyquist curves for the BS(SW)-SC and BS(AD)-SC devices, respectively.  d  CV curves for the BS(AD)-SC device heated at 70 °C.  e  displays a comparison of GCD curves for the BS(AD)-SC device operating at room temperature and at 70 °C

According to the reactions, with the use of the acid electrolyte in (3), the reaction consumes 8 protons (H + ). This “cleans” the surface by pulling the iron into the liquid solution, which is why we obtain a higher diffusion coefficient (9.51 × 10⁻⁸ cm²/s). While with seawater in (4), the reaction produces OH⁻ ions and solid Fe(OH)₂ (rust precursor). This solid “sludge” stays on the magnetite surface and could act as a physical barrier that slows down ion movement, resulting in your lower diffusion coefficient of 4.57 × 10⁻⁸ cm²/s. The order of magnitude for this diffusion coefficient agrees with previous reports for charge storage using redox reactions [ 54 ]. In supercapacitors of this type, the charge is not only stored on the surface, but the ions are also intercalated (inserted) into the solid matrix to react chemically. This value is generally several orders of magnitude faster than that in batteries because ions travel shorter distances within the active material layers.

Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) was employed to ascertain the Rs and Rct values, which are essential parameters obtained from an equivalent electrical circuit (typically the Randles circuit) to characterize the resistance components. Rs represents the resistance associated with the electrolyte, electrode materials, and contacts, whereas Rct denotes the resistance to charge transfer (whether electrons or ions) at the electrode/electrolyte interface. The determination of these two parameters was achieved through the analysis of Nyquist plots [ 55 ]. Figure  5 b and c present a series of Nyquist plots (with the inset image of the equivalent circuit in Fig.  5 b), from which the values of (Rs, Rct) were derived. The value pairs of (10.7 Ω, 1.2 Ω) and (0.25 Ω, 0.12 Ω) were obtained for the BS(SW)-SC and BS(AD)-SC devices, respectively. Moreover, Nyquist plot in Fig.  5 b shows a small semicircle in the range of 15–30 Ω on X-axis, which is characteristic of charge transfer processes limited by surface heterogeneity (frequency dispersion) [ 56 ]. From 30 Ω toward 50 Ω on the X-axis, the Nyquist curve changes slope, rising diagonally, indicating a diffusion regime (Warburg impedance) and capacitive behavior [ 57 ]. Additionally, Fig.  5 c shows that the intersection of the Nyquist plot corresponding to the BS(AD)-SC device intersects the X-axis very close to zero. This means a drastically higher system conductivity or extremely low internal ohmic resistance (Rs) compared to Fig.  5 b. In the high frequency region, it is observed a well-defined semicircle, suggesting a fast charge transfer process. In the low-frequency region for Fig.  5 c, a quasi-straight line is observed, and its slope is close to 45°, which is typical of an efficient ion diffusion and capacitive behavior. The literature indicates that lower Rct and Rs values enhance charge storage and extraction from the devices [ 58 ]. Consequently, the BS(AD)-SC device (which had the lowest resistance values) exhibited the highest capacitance.

Also, the influence of temperature on the electrochemical properties of the BS(AD)-SC device is presented. Figure  5 d illustrates the cyclic voltammetry curves obtained for the devices operating at 70 °C. The CV curves exhibited an increase in their width by 33%, attributed to the rise in temperature within the device. With rising temperatures, the electrolyte exhibits reduced viscosity, enhancing charge mobility and conductivity, which leads to a higher current, allowing ions to move more rapidly and leading to a considerable buildup of charge, enhancing both specific capacitance and the recorded current density [ 59 ]. Additionally, after the test at elevated temperature, the temperature decreased and returned to room temperature. After that process, a new electrochemical test was carried out. Fig. S3 in the supporting information displays the CV curves for the BS(AD)-SC device, which was cooled down to room temperature. The width of the curves was reduced with respect to their initial width. The recovery is indicative of the material’s stability under thermal stress, demonstrating that the electrochemical performance remained consistent even after exposure to elevated temperatures. Figure  5 e illustrates the GCD curves at a current density of 1 A/g for the BS(AD)-SC device, measured at 70 °C (black curve) and after return to room temperature and at room temperature (R.T.), see the red curve. The curves exhibited output voltages of 0.123 V and 0.145 V after 10 h in the GCD test, respectively. The specific capacitance (Cs) and energy density (Ed) values were calculated, yielding Cs/Ed values of 684.2 F/g and 95.1 Wh/kg for the high-temperature test, as well as 621.3 F/g and 135.3 Wh/kg for the room-temperature measurement. A slight increase in storage capacity was observed with the temperature and a minor decrease at room temperature, especially when compared to the findings prior to the temperature tests.

sections.heading: Raman, XPS and UV-Vis analysis for the determination of species for charge storage
paragraphs: The Raman analysis associated with graphene-based electrodes is presented in Fig.  6 . In carbon compounds, it exhibits two distinctive bands, labeled as the D and G bands, which range from 1200 to 1800 cm⁻¹ [ 60 ]. Vacancies and surface defects are associated with the D band. While the G band is related to C-C bonds in the crystal lattice. Besides, the numerical ratio (ID/IG) (it’s a value that gives an idea of the number of defects the sample may have) is determined by dividing the intensity of the D and G bands [ 61 ].
Fig. 6 a  Raman and  b  UV-Vis spectra for the BS-E electrode (before and after its use in devices containing SW and acidic electrolytes)

Figure  6 a illustrates the spectra of the BS-E, BS(SW)-E, and BS(AD)-E electrodes, with the D and G bands located at 1349.9 cm⁻¹ and 1584.6 cm⁻¹, respectively. The resulting numerical ratios were 0.11, 0.60, and 0.99, respectively. The results indicate that the maximum value of 0.99 for BS(AD)-E signifies a greater presence of defects in this electrode compared to the others, which recorded lower values. This would lead to enhanced electrochemical properties in the BS(AD)-SC device. Figure  6 b presents the UV-Vis spectroscopy analysis of three graphene-based electrodes with BS as a redox powder. This last figure presents the absorbance curve for the BS-E electrode, indicated by the black curve. The curve exhibits a pronounced absorption shoulder within the range of 200–250 nm that is attributed to silica (SiO₂) [ 62 ]. The absorbance in the 250–350 nm range is due to iron occupying different structural positions and is attributed to charge transfer transitions between Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ ions in magnetite [ 63 ]. Subsequently, the black sand electrode with seawater BS(SW)-E (see the red curve in Fig.  6 b) showed a broad absorption band ranging from 200 to 700 nm. This finding immediately revealed the electrode’s activation upon the addition of seawater compared to the black curve. Structural defects, including oxygen vacancies and broken Si-O/Fe-O bonds, which serve as anchors for Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions from the electrolyte, are found in the 200–350 nm range [ 64 ,  65 – 66 ]. Meanwhile, the formation of new iron oxide and hydroxide phases due to interaction with seawater is observed from 350 to 550 nm [ 67 ]. The highest absorbance intensity is observed in the 550–700 nm region, indicating a large number of defects (typical of surfaces). These increase the effective contact area, which is very useful for the type of energy storage used by EDL [ 68 ,  69 ]. On the other hand, the use of the acid electrolyte AD in the BS(AD)-E electrode (blue curve) breaks the Fe-O/Si-O bonds in the black sand, further increasing the number of defects [ 70 ]. Since these defects arise in the black sand electrode, this electrolyte will enhance the energy storage capacity of the device.

The chemical composition and oxidation state on the surface of the BS-E electrode (before and after use in the SC made with acidic electrolyte) were examined by the XPS technique. Figure  7 a displays the XPS spectra for the Fe 2p orbital in the electrode before/after use in the SC. Before use (top XPS spectrum in 7a), four main deconvoluted peaks were obtained with a Gaussian fitting method [ 71 ]. The signals encountered at 714.5 eV and 722.3 eV are attributed to iron in the oxidation state 2 +  (Fe²⁺), while the bands observed at 718.7 eV and 727.1 eV are related to the Fe³⁺ ionic species [ 72 ,  73 ,  74 – 75 ]. The electrode extracted from the used SC was studied, and its XPS spectrum for the Fe 2p orbital was re-evaluated (see the bottom XPS spectrum in Fig.  7 a). Nevertheless, an energy shift is observed in the deconvoluted bands. This results from lattice deformation, which can be caused by the existence of oxygen vacancies [ 76 ]. However, the XPS spectrum exhibits four bands located at 709.1 eV, 712.1 eV, 716.9 eV, and 724.8 eV, which correspond to the Fe²⁺ ionic species, Fe³⁺ (surface oxidation), the Fe²⁺ shake-up satellite band, and Fe³⁺, respectively [ 77 ,  78 ,  79 – 80 ]. Figure  7 b presents the XPS analysis in the electrode for the Si 2p orbital. The top spectrum corresponds to the electrode prior to being used in the supercapacitor. Three bands were deconvoluted from the XPS spectrum and were located at 103.5 eV, 104.2 eV, and 104.9 eV, which correspond to SiO₄⁴⁻, Si-𝞫, and residual Si-OH, respectively [ 81 ,  82 – 83 ]. The bottom spectrum in Fig.  7 b presents the XPS analysis for the electrode after use in the SC; three deconvoluted bands were observed. The signals were located at 101.8 eV, 102.7 eV, and 103.8 eV. The three bands mentioned were related to SiO, SiO x  (suboxides with x < 2), and SiO 2  formation [ 84 ,  85 – 86 ]. This silicate network is usually porous, which increases the specific surface area where the electrolyte charges accumulate. Silicon contributes to the physical part of storage (accumulation of ions on the surface by EDL), while iron contributes to the chemical part (redox reactions). On the other hand, Fig.  7 c shows the spectra of the O 1s orbital. The top part of Fig.  7 c corresponds to the spectra of the electrode before use in the SC; the signals were observed at 533.5 eV and 536.6 eV, which are related to chemisorbed H₂O and charging effects (due to certain silicates or quartz present in the black sand that act like insulators) [ 87 ]. The spectrum after use is presented in the bottom part of Fig.  7 c. Three deconvoluted signals were located at 531.8 eV, 532.9 eV, and 533.7 eV that are ascribed to oxygen vacancy defects, chemisorbed H₂O, and oxygen associated with silicate species SiO₂ [ 88 ,  89 – 90 ]. In summary, the composite system of magnetite and silicates in black sand (BS), together with oxygen vacancy defects, creates a hybrid material capable of delivering high specific capacitance and energy density (through redox reactions and EDL) along with excellent cyclic stability, positioning these natural sources of minerals as economical and efficient candidates for next-generation energy storage devices. Hence, the redox species for the charge storage in all the BS-based devices were oxygen vacancies, Fe 2+ /Fe 3+  and Si 4+ .
Fig. 7 XPS spectra recorded on the BS-E electrode (before and after its utilization in the BS(AD)-SC device made with acidic electrolyte):  a  Fe 2p,  b  Si 2p and  c  O1s orbitals

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Low-cost and efficient SCs were fabricated by using black sand (redox powder) and seawater (SW) electrolyte. The findings demonstrated that devices fabricated with seawater BS(SW)-SC displayed a capacitance of 282.24 F/g and energy density of 39.2 Wh/kg. In contrast, the BS(AD)-SC device made with acidic electrolyte achieved superior energy storage, with specific capacitance and energy density values of 668.66 F/g and 92.7 Wh/kg, respectively. To assess the stability, 1000 charge and discharge cycles were conducted. Consequently, the capacitance retention values for BS(SW)-SC and BS(AD)-SC devices decreased from 100% to 91.8% and from 100% to 95%, respectively. In addition, the capacitance retention of the BS(SW)-SC and BS(AD)-SC devices was also analyzed under mechanical stress; 1000 bending cycles were performed. In consequence, a decrease in capacitance from 100% to 90% and from 100% to 92% respectively, was observed. The capacitive/diffusive behavior of the best BS(AD)-SC device was investigated by Dunn’s method. The analysis yielded a b-value of 0.72, which suggests a hybrid storage mechanism. Also, to determine the ion kinetics (transport rate of mass) among the active materials (redox powder and electrolyte) within the electrode, the diffusion coefficient D was calculated. D values of 4.57 × 10⁻⁸ cm²/s and 9.51 × 10⁻⁸ cm²/s were obtained for devices made with seawater and acidic electrolyte. Thus, the D value for the device made with acidic electrolyte is 2.21 times higher than that for the device made with seawater. The devices were also studied at high operation temperatures. The results indicated that devices operating at 70 °C had a slight increase in storage capacity, with a specific capacitance and energy density of 684.2 F/g and 95.1 Wh/kg, respectively. Additionally, XPS analysis confirmed the presence of various redox centers, such as oxygen vacancies, Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺, and Si 4+ , for charge storage. Thus, the results of this research indicated that black sand (BS) with high content of iron oxide is a promising option for the construction of low-cost energy storage devices, which can be used for portable/wearable applications.
